note: Vol. I No. 18, and the issue that prints the Chicago post office's quarterly list of letters for 1 April 1834 — the month's census proxy, and the largest single cohort of named residents in this range. The list runs across two of the segmenter's strips and is claimed as two claims (c001, c002). THE ADVERTISING PAGES OF THIS ISSUE ARE A TESSERACT-FALLBACK READ: of thirty-two column strips only fourteen carry an independent Vision reading, and none of those fourteen is on page 3 or 4 where the advertisements are. Every claim below page 2 is therefore made against damaged text, and each says what it could not read rather than smoothing it.

claims.notes: THE PEOPLE OF CHICAGO ON 1 APRIL 1834, AS THE POST OFFICE HAD THEM — first half. This is the quarterly return of letters remaining in the Post Office at Chicago, and under ruling 1 every listed name mints a resident candidate. It is set across TWO of the segmenter's strips, so it is claimed as two claims: this one carries the alphabet from Abbott to Jackson, c002 carries Jacubus to Whittemore and the postmaster's signature. THE SAME LIST IS PRINTED AGAIN ON 16 APRIL (p4 cc2-3, claim c004 there) AND IS MINTED ONLY HERE, from the first printing, whose dateline is the list's own date — one list makes one cohort of people (T-0299, T-0292). Nine lines in this strip carry list debris that is not a name ('is Bet i', 'Bate es', 'Rowercee ee, i', 'shal astio', 'eeripeeancottric', 'inn Renny', 'pile. wr Bradley 2', 'é losept Habeax', 'Robt. V.’ Ale:') and are left unminted rather than guessed at; the 16 April reprint reads four of them — 'Josept Habeas', 'Robt. V. n', 'Nelson Brigham' and 'Robert W. Chapma[n]' — and c004 there records that without minting them a second time.

claims.notes: THE PEOPLE OF CHICAGO ON 1 APRIL 1834 — second half, and the postmaster who signs the return. Eighty-one names from Jacubus to Whittemore, then 'S..C. HOGAN, P.M.' — John S. C. Hogan, postmaster, who in this same month is also advertising as a storekeeper on his own account (1834-04-01 p3 c8, claim c006). TWO NAMES ARE READ DIFFERENTLY BY THE 16 APRIL REPRINT and the difference is recorded rather than resolved: this printing has 'Benjamin Reed,' and 'Ira Raymore' where the reprint has 'Benjarnin Smith' and 'Ira Saymoro'. Both sit between Salsby and Skinner in an alphabetical S-run, so the reprint's surname is the likelier reading on position alone — which is a judgement, not a witness, so 'Benjamin Reed' is minted as this printing has it and the alternative is written down here. Six lines carry debris rather than a name ('Mons: Kinbert', 'Win Lou!', 'iregory. 1', 'ee gear :', '« . Walker', 'Dr. Trimball' being illegible here) and are not minted; the reprint reads 'Mons. Lath', 'Ivin Lou', 'Gregory E. Legg', 'Dr. Trimball' and 'Geo. E. Walker' for five of them, recorded at c004 of 1834-04-16 without a second minting.

claims.notes: A STOREFRONT PLACED AGAINST GRAVES'S TAVERN. Botsford's whiskey advertisement gives no street, but it gives a neighbour, and Graves's tavern is the landmark this corpus already navigates by — the Board of Trustees met at 'the house of Charles Dexter Graves' on 4 December 1833 (T-0310, 1834-01-07 c001) and the blacksmithing shop of claim c004 below is 'opposite Graves' Tavern'. Three separate April advertisers place themselves against it, which is what a landmark is.

claims.notes: A BLACKSMITH'S SHOP OPPOSITE GRAVES'S TAVERN — AND A STREET NAME THAT IS NOT ON THE PLAT. The placement against the tavern is the usable part and is what this claim places. The street the advertisement names is 'Main-stre[et]', and the 1830 plat of Chicago has no Main Street; the quote keeps it rather than smoothing it to a street that does exist, because a reconstruction that quietly corrects its sources cannot be audited. Two readings are open and neither is asserted: the column is a Tesseract-fallback read and 'Main' may be OCR damage, or the paper may be printing a usage the plat does not carry. THE SECOND READING IS NOW THE BETTER ONE, and it is this pass's own corpus that says so: T-0291's read of September 1834 found a blacksmith advertising 'on Main-street, opposite the Tremont House' — a different smith, a different anchor, five months later, and the same street name. Two independent blacksmith advertisements in the same paper naming the same non-plat street is not OCR damage twice over; something in the Democrat's own usage calls a street Main, and that is worth a ticket rather than a silent correction. The advertisement is dated 26 November 1833 and is still running on 1 April 1834, which is a four-month window on the business.

The offset word is lost in this column — 'NE ast of i' is all the strip keeps of it — so the placement is recorded as street_only rather than as a relative one with an invented anchor. The advertisement is dated 20 January 1834 and is still running on 1 April, a ten-week window on the partnership.

claims.notes: A PARTNERSHIP DISSOLVES AND THE STORE STAYS OPEN. Brewster, Brewster & Hogan was dissolved by mutual consent on 20 February 1834 and the notice runs through April; the surviving partner — John S. C. Hogan, who is also the town's postmaster and signs the letter list at c002 — continues the business 'at the old stand'. That phrase is the reason this is worth a card: the trade moves to one name but the BUILDING does not move, so a storefront the reconstruction places for the firm stays placed for Hogan. The strip is a Tesseract-fallback read and the firm name itself is not legible in it; it is supplied from the fuller printing of the same notice on 1834-04-23 (p3 c8, 'pen d Co.' … 'BT BREWSTER. / FRAN, LIN BREWSTER, / JOHN 8. &- HOGAN..'), and the first Brewster's forename is not asserted from either.

claims.notes: THE MAIL TIMETABLE IS PRINTED AS A STANDING TABLE, and in April 1834 it is a Thursday-and-Saturday affair — the eastern mail arriving Thursdays at 6 A. M. and departing Saturdays. The column is a Tesseract-fallback read and the figures survive only in pieces, so nothing is asserted here beyond the days and the one hour the strip keeps whole; the value of the card is that the town's connection to the east was TWICE A WEEK at the scene date minus fifteen months, which is the kind of fact a walkthrough's post-office label needs and no map carries.
